place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the long dormitory bed

setup.zh: 腊月初八的夜。钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，给阿禾数出一百文。夜里，孙二狗摸到你铺前。
setup.en: The night of the eighth of the twelfth month. Money-Keeper Qian, packing up under the pagoda tree, counts a hundred cash out to A He. At night Sun Ergou creeps to your bunk.

recap.zh: 大比那夜，钱掌柜一文不少赔了阿禾一百文；孙二狗说：「是你拉的。」你给家里写了第一封信：「娘，漏勺也能打水。」木牌轻轻烫了一下——那张饼，还欠着。
recap.en: The night of the contest Money-Keeper Qian paid A He her hundred cash to the coin; Sun Ergou said, "You pulled me." You wrote your first letter home: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too." The token warmed, just a little — the flatbread is still owed.

en: "Ma, a skimmer can carry water too."

story.zh:
天黑下来的时候，钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊，看见阿禾过来，从怀里摸出一个小纸包，放在秤盘上称了一称，递给她：「阿禾姑娘。一文，一赔一百——你押的时候，板上写的是一赔一百。后来我要往上改，没改成，那是后来的事，跟你不相干。一百文，你数一数。」阿禾打开纸包，一文一文地数，数到一百，一文不多，一文不少。收摊的一个老弟子咂了咂嘴：「钱半文，钱半文。多一文不要，差半文不卖——这名号，倒不是白叫的。」钱掌柜把秤杆往肩上一扛，走了几步，回过头来冲小满道：「沈小满。明年还押你。」

小满道：「……他不是从来不认账的么？」阿禾道：「人人都这么说，可人人都没押中过。没押中过的人说他不认账，这话能信么？押中的人才知道。押中的人，又都不说。」那一文钱，是她娘缝在她衣角里的，初七那天她拿剪子挑开了线。她把一百文包好，塞进袖子里：「一百文，寄家，给弟弟。」顿了一顿，又道，「你今天没藏。」小满没说话。她翻开小本子记了一行，**利息：不收**，合上本子，只说了两个字：「藏好。」

那天夜里，人都睡下了以后，孙二狗摸到了小满的铺位跟前，蹲了好一会儿，才小声道：「沈师兄。第一轮……你是故意输给我的吧？」小满道：「不是。我脚滑。」孙二狗道：「五行台上的石头，是干的。」小满道：「我脚汗多。」孙二狗便不说话了。他从腰里解下那个蓝布包，断了的那根绳子，他已经拿线接上了，接得歪歪扭扭。他道：「沈师兄，我今天……倒了七回。我娘说，人倒了不丢人，倒了不起来才丢人。」他咧嘴笑了一下，扯着下巴上的伤，嘶了一口气，「台上倒了七回，起来了七回。下了台，在石阶上坐下去那一回……我是真起不来了。是你拉的。」小满没有说话。黑暗里，他听见孙二狗摸回了自己的铺位，躺下去的时候，还小声地念叨了一句：「……记着了。」隔了一会儿，黑地里又传来他的声音：「沈师兄，你会写字吧？」小满道：「会几个。」孙二狗道：「明天……你替我写一封信。我娘不识字，村里有个先生会念。你就写：娘，我赢了一场。」他顿了一顿，「别写是怎么赢的。」
story.en:
At nightfall Money-Keeper Qian was packing up under the pagoda tree. Seeing A He come, he took a small paper packet from his coat, weighed it on the scale and handed it to her: "Miss A He. One cash, one to a hundred — when you bet, the board said one to a hundred. Later I meant to raise it and didn't; that's later, nothing to do with you. A hundred cash — count it." She opened it and counted coin by coin to a hundred, not one more, not one less. A senior packing up nearby smacked his lips: "Qian Half-Cash, Qian Half-Cash. Won't take a cash over, won't sell a half-cash under — he's earned the name." Qian shouldered his steelyard, walked a few steps, and looked back at Xiaoman: "Shen Xiaoman. I'll bet on you next year."

"…Didn't they say he never pays?" "Everyone says so, and nobody's ever won. People who never won say he doesn't pay — can you believe that? Only the winners know. And the winners don't talk." That one cash her mother had sewn into her hem; on the seventh she'd snipped the thread. She wrapped up the hundred cash and tucked them into her sleeve: "A hundred cash, sent home, for my brother." A pause. "You didn't hide today." Xiaoman said nothing. She opened her notebook, wrote one line — **Interest: none charged** — closed it, and said just two words: "Hide well."

That night, when everyone was asleep, Sun Ergou crept to Xiaoman's bunk and crouched a long while before he whispered: "Brother Shen. The first round… you lost on purpose, didn't you?" "No. My foot slipped." "The stones on the platform are dry." "My feet sweat." Sun Ergou said no more. He untied the blue pouch; the snapped string he'd already mended with thread, crooked. "Brother Shen, today I… fell seven times. Ma says falling down's no shame; not getting up is." He grinned, pulled at the cut on his chin, and hissed. "Seven times down on the stage, seven times up. Off the stage, when I sat on the steps… I really couldn't get up. You pulled me." Xiaoman said nothing. In the dark he heard Sun Ergou feel his way back to his bunk, and as he lay down he murmured: "…I'll remember." After a while his voice came again out of the dark: "Brother Shen, you can write, can't you?" "A few words." "Tomorrow… write a letter for me. My ma can't read; there's a teacher in the village who'll read it to her. Just write: Ma, I won a bout." A pause. "Don't write how."

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next

story.zh:
孙二狗走了以后，小满趴在铺上，就着窗外的月光，给家里写第一封信。他头一句写的是「娘，我当上仙人了」，擦了；第二句写「娘，我打赢了马小宝」，想了想，这话要是传到村里，马三怕是要上门，又擦了。

小满在铺上一笔一笔地写：**娘：我进仙门了。一年五两，观里说腊月就送到家。屋顶修一修。盆可以收起来了，十七个都收。给我爹买一副护膝，狗皮的。给吴婆婆，再送一条鹿腿，这回是买的。我在这里很好。有人欺负我，我记着账。有几笔，已经还上了。——小满**

小满把信折好，想了想，又打开来，在最底下添了一行：**娘，漏勺也能打水。**信压在枕头底下，明天一早交给周衡，跟沈家那一包五两银子一车送下山。他握着胸口的木牌，小声道：「你欠我的那张饼……还欠着吧？」木牌轻轻地，烫了一下。像是在说：**还欠着。**

同是这一夜，西边几千里外，雍州太华山上，也有一个跟他同一年生的孩子没有睡：太一宫的真传赵昂。太一宫的年终大典从天黑做到三更：殿前那座台子又加了一层，石头是从山下一块一块背上来的，还没干透，台阶上结着白霜。九个真传穿着白衣排在台下，最末一个是赵昂，个子最矮，站得最直。大典之前，执事照例挨个儿验他们的身子：挽起袖子，掀开衣领，看有没有一道伤、一块疤——真传的身子金贵。验到赵昂，执事点了点头；台阶底下提灯的侍童里，替他挨过板子的阿槐，背还没好利索，直不起腰来，灯笼一晃一晃的。赵昂仰头看那座台，心想：等它通了天，我站在上头。

宫主东溟坐在殿上，一动也不动。他从来不站起来，也从来不伸手：递东西的是执事，传话的是执事，罚人的也是执事。每回开口之前，他都要抬起眼皮，往殿顶那一方天窗看一眼，像是在看天上有没有人在看他。这一回，他往天窗看了一眼，开口了：「昂，上来。」赵昂走上殿去，跪下。东溟道：「吾儿。」满殿的人都愣了——九个真传，他从来只叫名字。东溟又道：「明年秋，你去冀州。那边的水底下，有一样东西，该归太一宫。」一个执事替他问那句规矩里的话：「真传赵昂，可有二心？」

赵昂没有答。他从背上解下那口剑——师兄「下山了」以后，执事交给他的那一口——拧开剑鞘的底，从夹层里抽出一张叠成指甲大的纸条，师兄的字：**昂弟：台上冷，别上去。**他看了一眼，走到殿角的火盆跟前，当着东溟的面，扔了进去。纸条在火里卷了一卷，没了。他跪下：「没有。」台阶底下那盏灯笼，晃了一晃，又稳住了。东溟又往天窗看了一眼。那天夜里，一个执事端着玉碟进了他的屋子，捏开他的嘴，放进去一颗丹，不说是什么丹。他疼了一夜，天亮时筑了基。十三岁。他坐起来，头一件事，是摸了摸剑鞘的夹层。空的。那是他这辈子，唯一一封写给他的信。门外，阿槐端着一盆热水，弓着那道还没好的背，站了很久，才敢推门。
story.en:
When Sun Ergou had gone, Xiaoman lay on his bunk and by the moonlight at the window wrote his first letter home. The first line he wrote was "Ma, I've become an immortal" — rubbed out; the second, "Ma, I beat Ma Xiaobao" — he thought, if that got back to the village Ma San might come round, and rubbed it out too.

On his bunk Xiaoman wrote stroke by stroke: **Ma: I've entered the immortals' gate. Five taels a year; the temple says it'll reach home in the twelfth month. Fix the roof. The basins can be put away — all seventeen. Buy Pa a pair of kneepads, dog-skin. Send Granny Wu another leg of venison — bought, this time. I'm fine here. When people bully me, I keep accounts. A few are paid already. — Xiaoman**

Xiaoman folded the letter, thought, opened it again and added one line at the bottom: **Ma, a skimmer can carry water too.** He tucked it under his pillow; in the morning it would go to Zhou Heng and down the mountain on the same cart as the Shen family's five taels. Holding the token on his chest, he whispered: "That flatbread you owe me… still owed, right?" The token warmed, very lightly. As if to say: **Still owed.**

That same night, several thousand li to the west, on Mount Taihua in Yong, a boy born the same year as he was didn't sleep either: Zhao Ang, chosen disciple of the Palace of the Supreme One. The year-end rite of the Palace of the Supreme One ran from nightfall to the third watch: the platform before the hall had gone up another layer, its stones carried up from the foot of the mountain one by one, not yet dry, frost on its steps. Nine chosen disciples in white stood in a row below it, and the last was Zhao Ang, shortest, standing straightest. Before the rite the stewards checked each of their bodies as always: sleeves rolled up, collars turned back, looking for any wound or scar — a chosen disciple's body is precious. At Zhao Ang the steward nodded; among the lamp-bearing page boys at the foot of the steps, A Huai, who had taken the beating meant for him, still hadn't healed, he couldn't stand straight, and his lantern swayed. Zhao Ang looked up at the platform and thought: when it reaches heaven, I'll stand on top.

Dongming, the Palace Master, sat in the hall and did not move. He never stood, and he never reached out a hand: stewards passed things, stewards carried words, stewards did the punishing. Before he spoke he always raised his eyes to the skylight in the roof, as if to see whether anyone up there was watching him. This time he glanced at the skylight and spoke: "Ang. Come up." Zhao Ang went up into the hall and knelt. Dongming said: "My son." The whole hall froze — nine chosen disciples, and he only ever called them by name. Dongming went on: "Next autumn, you go to Ji. Under the water there is a thing that belongs to the Supreme One." A steward asked, for him, the question the rules required: "Chosen disciple Zhao Ang — have you a second heart?"

Zhao Ang didn't answer. He unslung the sword from his back — the one the stewards gave him after his senior brother "went down the mountain" — unscrewed the end of the scabbard and drew from its hollow a slip of paper folded to the size of a fingernail, in his senior brother's hand: **Brother Ang: it's cold up on the platform. Don't go up.** He looked at it once, went to the brazier in the corner, and before Dongming's eyes threw it in. The paper curled once in the fire and was gone. He knelt: "None." At the foot of the steps that one lantern swayed, and steadied. Dongming glanced at the skylight again. That night a steward came into his room with a jade dish, pried open his mouth and put in a pill, and didn't say what pill. He lay in pain all night and at dawn had built his foundation. Thirteen. He sat up, and the first thing he did was feel inside the scabbard. Empty. It had been the only letter anyone had ever written him. Outside the door, A Huai stood a long while with a basin of hot water, bent over his unhealed back, before he dared push it open.
